readerTitle: How many cupcakes before you make a cent?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (카페 납품용 컵케이크 제조 베이커리, 구독형 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 이익은 판매 한 건의 성질이 아니라 도달해야 하는 판매량이다. 고정비가 늘 때마다 그 기준선도 함께 움직인다.
misconception: 판매가가 원가보다 높으면 이익이 난다. 매출이 늘면 결국 흑자가 된다.

sources.text: 관리회계의 표준 개념 (손익분기점 = 고정비 ÷ 단위당 공헌이익)

cards.title: Every cupcake makes money. The bakery doesn't.
body: A small bakery makes cupcakes for local cafés. It sells each one for $2.00. Flour, butter, boxes and delivery fuel cost $0.80.
So every cupcake leaves $1.20. Last month the bakery sold 8,000 of them and still lost $2,400.

image.label: Profit starts only after the fixed-cost pile is covered.
image.brief: 따뜻한 톤의 작은 제빵 공장 내부. 컵케이크가 가득한 철제 랙과 배달용 상자들. 랙 위에 작은 칠판이 걸려 있고 "Last month: −$2,400"이라고 빨간 분필로 쓰여 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: When does the bakery stop losing money?
body: Rent, two bakers' wages, the van lease and the oven loan come to $12,000 a month. They stay the same whether the bakery makes 1 cupcake or 10,000.
How many cupcakes a month does it need to sell to stop losing money?

options.feedback: That divides fixed costs by the $2 price. But $0.80 of every cupcake goes to ingredients and delivery, so only $1.20 is left to pay the rent.
Right. Each cupcake leaves $1.20 toward the $12,000. 12,000 ÷ 1.20 = 10,000.
A safe-sounding guess, but it divides by the $0.80 cost. What pays the fixed costs is the $1.20 left over, so the target is lower.

cards.title: Why 8,000 cupcakes lose money.
cards.callout: At 10,000 cupcakes, the money left over is exactly $12,000. Each cupcake after that adds $1.20 of profit.

cards.title: Break-even point
body: The **break-even point** is the sales volume where you stop losing money but haven't made any yet. Below it, you lose. Above it, you profit.
Break-even = fixed costs ÷ what each sale leaves after its own costs.
So profit isn't something each sale has. It's a volume you have to reach first.

image.label: Graph where a rising sales line crosses a flat fixed-cost line
image.brief: 단순한 손익분기 그래프. 가로축 "Cupcakes per month", 세로축 "$". 수평선 "Fixed costs $12,000", 우상향 직선 "Money left over from sales". 두 선이 만나는 지점에 "Break-even: 10,000" 표시. 교차점 왼쪽 영역은 연한 빨강 "Loss", 오른쪽은 연한 초록 "Profit".

cards.title: More sales, still a loss.
body: A café chain offers a big order. Sales would jump from 8,000 to 12,000 cupcakes a month. The owner celebrates: that's well past 10,000.
But baking and delivering 12,000 needs a third baker and a second van, costing $3,000 more each month. Fixed costs rise to $15,000, so break-even moves to **12,500**.
At 12,000 cupcakes, the bakery now loses $600. The growth moved the finish line.

image.label: Add a cost and the break-even volume moves out.
image.brief: 일러스트. 배달 밴이 결승선 쪽으로 달리는데, 작업복 차림의 인물 둘(새 제빵사, 두 번째 밴)이 결승선 테이프를 뒤로 옮기고 있음. 원래 위치에 "10,000", 새 위치에 "12,500" 라벨. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Every new fixed cost has its own break-even.
body: Before adding any fixed cost, ask: how many extra sales pay for this alone? At $1.20 a cupcake:
list: A $3,000 baker and van need 2,500 more
cards.callout: If you can't say where those extra sales will come from, the new cost moves you backward.

cards.title: A break-even number is only as good as its guesses.
body: It assumes price and per-unit costs hold steady. Win volume with a discount, and each sale leaves less, so break-even rises.
It ignores cash timing. Cafés that pay 60 days late can leave you short of cash even above break-even.
And it says nothing about demand. Needing 10,000 cupcakes doesn't mean 10,000 buyers exist.

cards.title: Now it's a subscription app.
body: Your app charges $20 a month. Servers, payment fees and support cost about $4 per user. The team and tools cost $48,000 a month, so you break even at 3,000 paying users. You have 2,400.
A salesperson would cost $8,000 a month. When does hiring make sense?

options.text: Hire now. More sales effort always gets you closer to break-even
options.feedback: You gain sales capacity, but the hire pushes break-even up to 3,500 users. Without enough new users, you end up further from profit.

options.text: Hire only if they can realistically add well over 500 users who stay
options.feedback: 500 users × $16 covers the $8,000 salary. Only users beyond that move you toward profit, and only if they don't cancel.

options.text: Hire if they can add about 400 paying users
options.feedback: That divides $8,000 by the $20 price. Each user leaves $16 after their own costs, so it takes 500 just to pay for the hire.

cards.title: Profit starts at a number, not at a price.
body: Break-even = fixed costs ÷ what each sale leaves after its own costs. Recheck it every time you add a fixed cost.
**Try it today:** add up one month of your fixed costs. Divide by what one typical sale leaves. Is your usual monthly volume above or below that line?
